# FindByField

Finds the first object in an array whose field passes a comparison.

## Signature

```jyro
# fragment
FindByField(items, fieldName, operator, value)
```

| Parameter | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `items` | array | The array to search. Null is read as an empty array. Any other type that is not an array is a runtime error. |
| `fieldName` | string | The name of the field to compare, one key as written: a name with a dot in it is never read as a path. A number or a boolean is read as its string form, and null as the empty string. |
| `operator` | string | The comparison, one of `"=="`, `"!="`, `"<"`, `"<="`, `">"` and `">="`, with the field on the left and value on the right. Any other value, null included, is a runtime error, raised before any element is examined, even for an empty array. |
| `value` | any | The value to compare each field with. Any value, null included. |

## Returns

Any. The first object, in array order, whose field passes the comparison: the element itself, not a copy. Null when no object passes, including for an empty array.

## Remarks

Elements that are not objects are passed over. A field the object does not have is read as null. With `"=="` and `"!="` values are compared as the `==` operator compares them, so a null field equals null. With the other operators a null field never passes; otherwise both sides must be numbers or both strings (strings compared code unit by code unit), and any other pair is a runtime error.

## Example

`FindByField([{ "id": 1 }, { "id": 2 }], "id", "==", 2)` returns `{ "id": 2 }`.
